newsitem.title: USA: SF Fed study finds fault with opportunistic policy.
newsitem.headline: SF Fed study finds fault with opportunistic policy.

text.p: A new monetary policy approach called "opportunistic disinflation" raises credibility problems that may offset some of the perceived benefits of the strategy, according to an economist at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco.
"There is an obvious tension between credibility and opportunism," Glenn Rudebusch, research officer at the San Francisco Fed, wrote in the latest issue of the bank's weekly Economic Letter.
"The public may be skeptical about the importance or validity of an ultimate inflation target when it is promulgated but not acted upon by an opportunistic central bank," Rudebusch added.

Opportunistic disinflation, a strategy that attempts to make use of recessions in the fight against inflation, was outlined in a recent paper by two Fed economists and is favored by some officials at the central bank.

Under that approach, policymakers would not actively seek to achieve further gains against inflation when it is already low. Instead, they would wait for the inevitable recession to wring out price pressures naturally.
However, if inflation appeared to be at risk of increasing, opportunistic policymakers would aggressively fight it.
Rudebusch contrasted the opportunistic strategy to inflation targeting, which he said was preferable.
In both approaches, he pointed out, policy makers' ultimate goal is price stability, assumed by many economists to be an annual rise in the Consumer Price Index of around 1 percent.

However, Rudebusch noted, except when inflation is high the "interim" goal of opportunism is simply the current inflation rate, which could raise questions about the commitment to achieving the longer-run price stability goal.
Working toward specific inflation targets in the interim as opposed to waiting for accidental developments such as a recession would boost credibilty and yield economic benefits, Rudebusch said.

"If people believe that inflation will fall, then inflation may be reduced with a smaller transitional cost in terms of lost output and employment," he said. "In this way, anticipated disinflations may be less painful than unanticipated ones."
Rudebusch said past research by the Fed board suggests that if policy were not credible, then the cost in terms of unemployment of reducing inflation could be twice as high.
"Of the two new strategies for monetary policy, it appears that credibility would be better achieved with inflation targets than with opportunistic policy," Rudebusch said.
"Inflation targets provide a transparent, accountable, deliberate path to price stability -- attributes lacking in an opportunistic approach."
